To defeat our enemies, we may use their weapons against them. It is important not to allow them to control the narrative, nor allow them to set the definitions and parameters of the discussion. That does mean that we have to surpass them in execution. We have to make our terms and concepts more digestible, more palatable, and more resonant with the reader. Our meaning must have emotional and visceral appeal. The reader must want to believe us. If we are offensive or combative, or derogatory, the reader "shuts down" and we make no progress. And remember, our message often should not be primarily attempting to convert the opposition in the debate, but to persuade the reader. Laptop upgrades:

I bought a tower off craigslist that had an older i7 and mother board. I put the power supply, ram and hard drive in from spare parts. I ended up spending $175, later put in $100 for more ram and $80 on a used graphics card.

It really depends on your budget, and your requirements. If you're looking for another laptop, you'll want to set aside at least $1200 to get yourself a halfway decent gaming laptop. As a rule, laptops are rarely very upgradable.

If you're looking for a desktop, about $1000 or more will get you a very good system. $800 will get you a decent mid-level box. $600 or less will get you something you'll want to throw out a window. My advice is to go as far to the high end as possible. Intel i5 or better (avoid i3 as it's weak, avoid i7 unless you do non-gaming workhorse operations that can take advantage of it), geforce 960 or 970 with at least 2gb vram, and 8 - 12 gb of system ram. You could shave more money off by going with AMD hardware, but trust me when I say you're not doing yourself a favor.

Yeah, I second all of this, also I have never had problems with Asus laptops or Parts, Acer I only use then monitors and had a AMD laptop with crap video drivers. Basically stay away from Dell,Lenovo, and HP.

Honestly, if you're asking this question you probably shouldn't be trying to upgrade a laptop on your own. If you're looking to pick out a new one Asus and Acer usually have high-end laptops at competitive prices. If the form factor isn't too much of an issue for you then you can build your own high-end desktop for ~$1k, though I recommend something closer to $1.5k for the sake of future proofing.

Laptops can be incredibly finicky and vary a lot from model to model. Building a desktop, though, is basically just round peg into the round hole, square peg into the square hole.

If you go this route, sadly, v/buildapc is pretty dead but the good news is that the cancer on that other site hasn't spread to /r/buildapc. Work out your budget, poke through Amazon and New Egg for some good parts, then post your proposed rig over there for feedback.

A few basic pointers: an SSD is an absolute must these days but an M.2/PCI-E is overkill, a single mid-to-high-end card with SLI/Crossfire (e.g. the GTX970) is good nice you can pick up a second card when the first one is getting dated and get a lot of extra mileage. You probably only need 8GB of RAM at the moment, but you should prepare to upgrade to 12 or 16 at some point during your computer's lifespan. For the sake of future proofing you probably want a power supply in the 750W range and make sure it's certified. 4k monitors are kind of overkill at the moment and a card like the one I recommended will have trouble keeping up with it; 1440p (or "quad HD") seems to be the sweet spot at the moment. Sorry for rambling, I love this stuff and never get a chance to build high end machines for work.
